teaser: Below the first rules, an agent's behaviour policy is the business: functions, processes, clients, values. Layered, owned, counted, and where vendors plug in.
core_idea: The first rules written for an agent are mechanical and vendors enforce them well, but every layer above them is the company's own business logic: how a function is done, the steps a process goes through, who a client is right now, and what the company is for; much of that logic was never written down because software enforced it by omission, and agents working through APIs bypass that; a behaviour policy built in layers, each refining the one below with its own owner, can hold it, can count how much of it is backed by a control, by an accepted risk or by hope, and gives vendors a written rule to enforce and a number to move, which is what lets the business hand work to agents and scale.

nodes.label: The bottom layers are mechanics
nodes.summary: Own account, secrets held by the platform, tools switched off, sending needs a person: boundaries vendors enforce well.

nodes.label: send_message ran with no prompt
nodes.summary: The measured Gmail deployment: thirty tools, sending unprompted, trashing behind an approval. Mechanics need measuring.

nodes.label: Above the mechanics is the business
nodes.summary: Function, process, relationship and organisation layers, each a set of rules a manager would say out loud, each with its own owner.

nodes.label: Vendors cannot model each customer's business
nodes.summary: To scale they build what is the same for everybody; the business layers differ per company and are often unwritten.

nodes.label: Software was the law
nodes.summary: Approval chains, RBAC and workflows encoded the rules; a missing button was a control.

nodes.label: Agents work through the API, not the screen
nodes.summary: The rule the interface enforced by omission is no longer enforced unless it is written down.

nodes.label: Policies inside policies
nodes.summary: Each layer refines the one below inside the room it allows, from tool permissions up to what the company is for.

nodes.label: Shared facts, own formulas, declared bridges
nodes.summary: The ABP vocabulary's three layers: customers extend it in their own vault without changing the shared one.

nodes.label: Control, accepted risk, or hope
nodes.summary: Each rule is backed by a boundary, governed by a named acceptance with an expiry, or resting on hope; the counts are the finding.

nodes.label: Five, six and six of seventeen
nodes.summary: In the fictional firm the platform layer is all control and the organisation layer all hope.

nodes.label: A vendor control moves one written rule
nodes.summary: Send gateways, content checks, ledger approvals and blocked-recipient lists each move a rule from hope or acceptance to control.

nodes.label: Frameworks already ask for the description
nodes.summary: AI BCF RG.2 asks that what an autonomous system does is described; AC.3 asks for a named owner.

nodes.label: The upper layers read like skills
nodes.summary: A skill says how; a policy layer says what is allowed, who owns it and what stands in the way. Together they codify the business.

nodes.label: A real inbox, layered and counted
nodes.summary: Write the upper layers above the measured Gmail deployment, publish the counts, then again with a vendor's control in the path.

quotes.text: The rule that the user interface enforced by omission is no longer enforced, unless somebody writes it down and something enforces it.
quotes.why: Why agents force business logic out of software and into policy.

quotes.text: A control attached to a written rule is worth more than one switched on in general, because the customer can see what it bought.
quotes.why: Why the behaviour policy is a good integration point for vendors.
